A Taylor series is a power series expansion of a function centered at a point, built from the function's derivatives. It takes the form: f of x equals f of a plus f prime of a times x minus a, plus f double prime of a times x minus a squared over two factorial, plus f triple prime of a times x minus a cubed over three factorial, and so on. A Maclaurin series is a special case: a Taylor series centered at x equals zero. Taylor series are the bridge between polynomial approximation and transcendental functions, allowing you to approximate sine of x, e to the x, or natural log of x locally with polynomials.

The general formula is: f of x equals the sum from n equals zero to infinity of f to the nth derivative at a, divided by n factorial, times x minus a to the n. The n-th derivative of f at a, divided by n factorial, gives the coefficient of x minus a to the n. For a Maclaurin series centered at zero, the formula becomes the sum from n equals zero to infinity of f to the nth derivative at zero, divided by n factorial, times x to the n.

Several canonical examples are essential. E to the x equals one plus x plus x squared over two factorial plus x cubed over three factorial, and so on—this Maclaurin series converges for all x. Sine of x equals x minus x cubed over three factorial plus x to the fifth over five factorial minus x to the seventh over seven factorial, and so on, also converging for all x. Cosine of x equals one minus x squared over two factorial plus x to the fourth over four factorial minus x to the sixth over six factorial, and so on, converging everywhere. Natural log of one plus x equals x minus x squared over two plus x cubed over three minus x to the fourth over four, and so on, but this one converges only for x between negative one and one, excluding negative one.

Taylor series converge within a radius of convergence—the interval where the series actually equals the original function. When you truncate a series after n terms, the error is bounded by the Lagrange remainder or integral remainder.

Taylor series are the hidden backbone of scientific computing. When a calculator computes sine of zero point five or e to the second, it is likely using a truncated Taylor series. In theoretical mathematics, Taylor series let you study a function through its derivatives—smoothness, singularities, and local behavior all show up in the coefficients. They are foundational to perturbation theory in physics: approximate a hard problem by starting with a simpler one and adding corrections term by term. Quiz-bowl questions test writing the first few terms of a Maclaurin series, recognizing which functions match which series, and applying series to compute limits or approximations.
